papers.title: Coding region changes in the Hippo pathway component YAP1 contribute to body size differences among mammalian species
papers.abstract: Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila, and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

papers.title: Delta/Notch signaling level is decoded through transcriptional burst duration during muscle progenitor specification
papers.abstract: The ability of progenitor cells to interpret different levels of signaling pathway activity is fundamental to the generation of cellular diversity during development. Muscle progenitors, for example, are exposed to different levels of signals from their microenvironment. However, how they decode these quantitative differences to regulate their cellular behaviors during myogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we addressed this question during the specification of two populations of Drosophila adult muscle progenitors (AMPs). We found that, despite being spatially adjacent, indirect flight muscle (IFM) and direct flight muscle (DFM) progenitors receive distinct levels of Notch signaling. We further show that the spatial distribution of epithelial Delta contributes to differential Notch activation. Higher Delta levels adjacent to IFM progenitors promote stronger Notch signaling. To investigate how these quantitative differences are translated into transcriptional responses, we developed a Notch-responsive MS2 reporter to monitor transcription in living AMPs. Our measurements reveal that Notch-dependent transcription occurs in stochastic bursts, with IFM progenitors displaying longer but less frequent bursts than DFM progenitors. Strikingly, equalizing epithelial Delta levels abolished differences between the two populations in both Notch-dependent transcriptional activity and the protein levels of Notch target genes. Together, our findings suggest that quantitative differences in signaling may be translated into distinct transcriptional outputs through modulation of transcriptional bursting. This may represent a mechanism by which a single signaling pathway can be deployed to regulate diverse cellular responses during development.

papers.title: From cellular stress to cytokine modulation: An in vitro study of intestinal effects of major Alternaria mycotoxins
papers.abstract: Mycotoxins are frequently detected in food, making the gastrointestinal tract the first organ exposed. Here, we used various in vitro intestinal cell models to explore the barrier and immune responses to the Alternaria mycotoxins alternariol (AOH), alternariol methyl ether (AME), altenuene (ALT), altertoxin I (ATX-I), tentoxin (TEN), and tenuazonic acid (TeA). The mycotoxins exhibited low toxicity in undifferentiated Caco-2 cells, but AOH, AME, and ATX-I affected the cell cycle and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. None of the toxins alone or in combination with IL-1beta; had any effect on the barrier integrity or viability of the differentiated Caco-2/HT29-MTX-E12 co-culture. Furthermore, AOH and AME reduced IL-1beta-induced IL-8 secretion, whereas TeA increased the secretion, demonstrating immunomodulatory effects. For verification, we used the more in vivo-like EpiIntestinal TM model, which is based on human primary cells. AOH, AME, and TeA had minor effects on viability without compromising barrier integrity; also, cytokine secretion was less affected than in the co-culture model. Studies on uptake confirmed low absorption of AOH, AME, and TeA. Overall, the studies indicate a low absorption and moderate effects of the toxins on the gastrointestinal tract.

papers.title: Evaluation of immunotoxic effects and metabolism of enniatins and beauvericin using in vitro models of the human intestinal epithelium
papers.abstract: Enniatins (ENNs) and beauvericin (BEA) are mycotoxins produced by Fusarium species. They are frequently detected in cereal-based foods such as maize and wheat. Consequently, the gastrointestinal tract is a primary site of exposure for consumers of grain-containing foods. This study examined intestinal effects of four major ENNs: ENNB, ENNB1, ENNA, and ENNA1, and the structurally related mycotoxin BEA, using the primary human intestinal model EpiIntestinal (TM) tissues and a Caco-2/TH29-MTX-E12 co-culture. None of the compounds induced cytotoxicity or impaired the barrier integrity at concentrations ranging from 1 to 10 microM. Furthermore, all ENNs and BEA stimulated IL-6 secretion, with ENNA and ENNA1 inducing the strongest responses, while IL-8 secretion was only triggered by ENNA and ENNA1. Transport studies revealed that approximately 32% of ENNB and 25% of ENNB1 crossed from the apical to the basolateral side of the intestinal tissue within 4 h, whereas the other ENNs and BEA had transport ratios below 10%. Further findings suggested that uptake and intracellular accumulation of ENNs and BEA were influenced by their affinity to the efflux transporter P-glycoprotein (P-gp). In addition, several ENNB and ENNB1 metabolites were generated in the EpiIntestinal (TM) tissues and transported. Lastly, it was demonstrated that ENNB can disturb the metabolism of the sex hormone estradiol in human liver microsomes. Overall, ENNs and BEA showed limited acute toxicity in human intestinal models but elicited distinct inflammatory responses and differed in transport and metabolism. These findings may be of relevance when evaluating health risks from chronic, low-level dietary exposure

papers.title: Effect of Varying Cigarette Smoke Concentrations and Durations on the Retinal Pigment Epithelium
papers.abstract: Dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of blindness in the elderly, and treatment options are limited. Cigarette smoke (CS), the primary modifiable environmental risk factor for AMD, damages the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) by inducing oxidative stress, which in turn activates multiple stress response pathways. Low levels of stress induce autophagy, a cell-recycling mechanism; moderate stress induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT); and high, sustained stress, once other cytoprotective pathways are exhausted, leads to cell death. All three pathways are implicated in AMD pathogenesis. Although CS is known to induce oxidative stress, its impact on these distinct stress response pathways remains understudied, and few studies have directly compared mouse and human RPE responses to the same stressor. Here, we examined the effect of varying concentrations and durations of cigarette smoke condensate (CSC) exposure on oxidative stress, autophagy, EMT, and cell death in ARPE-19 (human) and mouse RPE (MRPE) cells. Understanding which stress response pathways predominate at which CSC exposure levels may help guide the development of AMD treatments stratified by smoking history.

papers.title: Autophagy activator AA-20 engages CDK5 to promote lipophagy and improve neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes
papers.abstract: Lipophagy, the selective degradation of lipid droplets (LDs) by autophagy, has the potential to ameliorate neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's (PD) and Alzheimer's (AD), wherein LD accumulation has been linked to the exacerbation of the proteinopathy component of neurodegeneration. Pharmacological lipophagy inducers remain scarce. We previously identified AA-20 as a novel autophagy activator that acts independently of mTORC1 inhibition, thereby providing a means of stimulating autophagy while avoiding the immunosuppressive side effects associated with direct mTORC1 inhibition. Prior work also showed that AA-20 treatment reduces PolyQ aggregate levels in several C. elegans tissues. Here, we demonstrate that AA-20 enhances LD recruitment to autophagosomes and promotes LD degradation via lysosomal acid lipase activation in murine hippocampal neuronal cells, consistent with lipophagy activation. In human Swedish Amyloid Precursor Protein mutated cerebral organoids, two weeks of AA-20 treatment normalized aberrant lipidomic profiles by selectively reducing various disease-associated lipids, while also correcting the AD-associated electrical hyperexcitability phenotype. Moreover, we identified cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), a neuronal kinase linked to AD hyperexcitability and PD pathology, as a target of AA-20. AA-20-induced autophagy and lipid clearance in HT22 cells require CDK5. In a neuronal seeding model of -synuclein pathology, AA-20 reduced pS129--synuclein levels. Collectively, these findings indicate AA-20 can promote lipophagic clearance of LDs and mitigate multiple cellular phenotypes associated with lipidopathy and proteinopathy in neurodegenerative disease models.

papers.title: Cross-regulatory sRNA networks shape adaptive stress responses in Staphylococcus aureus: RsaC and RsaOI regulate galactose metabolism and cell wall homeostasis
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen whose adaptability relies on network of regulators, including two-component systems, transcription factors and small regulatory RNAs. Yet most of these regulators are dispensable for growth, suggesting cooperation or redundancy between them. To explore this hypothesis, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen of 43 TFs against the promoters of seven sRNAs, which identified 27 novel TF-sRNA promoter interactions. We then focused on three sRNAs. We showed that srn_9342 is repressed by VraR and MntR, which also control rsaOI and rsaC, respectively. We found that rsaC, like rsaOI, is induced by acidic pH and vancomycin exposure, whereas srn_9342 expression remained unchanged. We also demonstrated in vitro that Srn_9342 interacts with both RsaOI and RsaC. Its role toward these two sRNAs remains unknown, but this interaction raises the possibility that it modulates their availability or activity. RsaOI and RsaC both act on the tagatose pathway for galactose utilization, through different genes: lacD for RsaOI, as previously reported, and lacC for RsaC, newly identified here. We showed that both sRNAs are required for surface charge remodeling and for growth under subinhibitory vancomycin. They also modulate the virulence factors PSM and protein A. Both sRNAs reduce PSM production, whereas protein A is decreased by RsaOI, likely through Rot, and increased by RsaC through an unknown, probably indirect mechanism. Together, our results suggest that a single cell wall stress can engage several regulators that could cooperate on shared targets or pathways, which may explain why individual regulators are dispensable.

papers.title: Tripartite toxin-antitoxin system regulates the production and release of pneumolysin by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
papers.abstract: The production of toxins is critical to the success of bacteria, with their targets and outcomes varying widely. Pneumolysin (Ply), produced by the major human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae, is a cytolytic pore forming toxin that plays many diverse roles including inducing tissue damage and inflammation, evasion of many aspects of the human immune system, invasion of the bacteria into deeper tissue, and transmission to new hosts. Despite its importance, many aspects of the biology of this toxin have to date remained unknown, in particular, what role of the three other genes that form part of the ply operon play in Ply production. Here we demonstrate that these genes encode a complex regulatory system, that includes a putative membrane destabilising protein (PlyA) and a MazEF-like toxin-antitoxin system (PlyB and PlyC), the toxin of which (PlyC) destabilises the Ply transcript. We propose a tripartite model whereby when the operon reaches relatively high levels of expression PlyA destabilises the S. pneumoniae membrane creating a stress that triggers a necessary negative feedback loop which results in the degradation of the PlyB antitoxin, release of the PlyC toxin and degradation of the ply transcript, thereby providing a means by which Ply production can be tightly regulated. Given the importance of Ply to the ability of S. pneumoniae to cause infection, identifying the factors that result in the shutdown of Ply production and release by the bacteria would seem promising target for future therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Butyrate reverts Chlamydia pneumoniae -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
papers.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extra intestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of C. pneumoniae or C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with C. trachomatis-infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated. C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping Chlamydia-host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Age Associated Shifts Toward Anaerobic Taxa and Amino Acid Degradation Potential in the Canine Oral Microbiome
papers.abstract: Introduction: Periodontal disease is common in dogs and is associated with changes in oral microbial community composition. How the canine oral microbiome restructures across age at both ecological and metabolic levels remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We analyzed shotgun metagenomic buccal-swab profiles from 1,125 dogs using MetaPhlAn. Functional profiles from HUMAnN were analyzed at pathway and functional-group levels. We annotated species-level taxa with oxygen preference and evaluated oxygen-tolerant and anaerobic taxa abundances across age. We also characterized community structure, metabolic potential, Shannon diversity, and age and weight prediction using nested cross-validated Elastic Net models. Results: Age was associated with substantial restructuring in the oral microbiome. Mean oxygen-tolerant taxa abundance decreased from 67.5% in puppies to 29.1% in mature dogs, whereas anaerobic abundance increased from 14.3% to 53.8%. The oxygen-tolerant: anaerobe log-ratio declined with age (Spearman {rho} = -0.616). Metabolic profiles also varied with age, with higher amino-acid-degradation potential and lower glycolysis and central-carbohydrate potential, and aerobic-respiration-I abundance in older dogs. Shannon diversity increased with age ({rho} = 0.537, p < 0.001). Elastic Net models trained on microbiome species abundance predicted age (Pearson r = 0.609; R-squared = 0.371) and weight (r = 0.498; R-squared = 0.248) with moderate accuracy. Discussion: Canine age was associated with coordinated changes in oral-community oxygen preference and metabolic pathways. These findings extend prior taxon-specific observations by examining a broader ecological shift and metabolic potential in the canine oral microbiome. This provides a reference for future longitudinal or clinical studies of oral maturation and periodontal disease.

papers.title: Ambivalent roles of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay in heat stress tolerance
papers.abstract: RNA homeostasis is essential for gene regulation and cellular survival; however, how RNA degradation pathways contribute to stress adaptation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in regulating heat stress (HS) memory in a long-term acquired thermotolerance assay. NMD-deficient Arabidopsis thaliana mutants upf1-5 and upf3-1 exhibited a biphasic phenotype: they displayed transiently elevated heat tolerance during early recovery but became more sensitive to heat during late recovery. Genetic analysis of upf3;hsfa2 and upf3;hsfa3 double mutants demonstrated that the early heat tolerance occurs independently of both HsfA2 and HsfA3 HS-memory transcription factors. Under non-treated conditions, the upf3-1 transcriptome exhibited baseline priming of heat-shock responsive transcripts, likely accounting for the initial heat tolerance. Further transcriptome profiling revealed that upf3-1 mutants exhibited reduced levels of the functional HsfA2 isoform (HsfA2-I) and attenuated expression of the HsfA2-dependent thermomemory regulon following the triggering stress. NMD deficiency also upregulated immune-response genes while repressing developmental and cell-wall-associated pathways. Together, impaired HsfA2-dependent thermomemory and a compromised growth defense balance underlies the late heat sensitivity of NMD deficient plants. Overall, NMD acts as a dual-action post-transcriptional regulator that coordinates the transition from stress response to growth resumption.

papers.title: Minimal requirements and evolution of polar membrane targeting in the land plant SOSEKI protein family
papers.abstract: Accurate spatial distribution of polar proteins is essential for cell function, but mechanisms underlying polar protein targeting in plants are poorly understood. Here, we dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying the polar targeting of the SOSEKI1 (SOK1) protein in Arabidopsis thaliana. Using extensive mutagenesis and truncation analyses of the polarity domain, we mapped the minimal polarity fragment necessary and sufficient for stable polar targeting to a 25-amino-acid region. This region likely forms an amphipathic helix, and mutations reveal that both its polar and apolar faces are essential for membrane association and polarity. Using phylogenetic analysis, we reconstruct the evolutionary history of the minimal polar targeting region across land plants. Using cross-species expression and protein localization, we infer the ancestral polar SOK localization pattern and show how it remained remarkably conserved, only to diversify upon gene duplication. This work identifies a polar targeting peptide in plants, reveals a mechanism for polar membrane targeting of a plant protein family, and demonstrates both conservation and diversification within this family.

papers.title: Quantifying subcellular organization from localization to co-occurrence with InSpace
papers.abstract: Cell identity and function depend not only on molecular abundance, but also on how molecules are organized within cells. Although spatial transcriptomics now resolves individual RNA molecules within cells, routine computational workflows reduce these measurements to cell-by-gene count matrices, retaining abundance while discarding information about intracellular localization and molecular co-occurrence. This loss of spatial information creates a need for scalable methods that preserve subcellular detail and enable comparisons across diverse cellular morphologies. Therefore, we present InSpace, a scalable framework for quantifying these complementary dimensions of subcellular organization. InSpace-R maps transcripts onto a continuous radial coordinate anchored to nuclear and cell boundaries, while InSpace-C measures distance-dependent co-occurrence or depletion of molecular pairs. Simulations and orthogonal biochemical references support accurate measurements, with scalability demonstrated on datasets containing 275 million transcripts. RNA-RNA and RNA-DNA analyses recover organelle-linked neighbourhoods and associations between nascent transcripts and their genomic origins. Analysis of B and plasma cells across 58 tumour datasets spanning 12 cancer types reveals that reduced MHC-II transcript abundance accompanies more peripheral localization and stronger mutual co-occurrence, separating these transcripts from a program enriched for ER-targeted proteins. InSpace makes intracellular organization accessible alongside abundance, enabling discovery of spatial programs that distinguish cellular states and generate hypotheses about their functional specialization.

papers.title: Efficient growth factor production stabilizes cooperation in a cellular public goods game
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic cells secrete growth factors that facilitate the proliferation and survival of neighboring cells in a coordinated manner essential for tissue development, repair, and homeostasis. However, mutant cells that fail to produce these factors may exploit the benefits provided by neighboring producers, thereby gaining a proliferative advantage that could lead to the extinction of the producer clone. Evolutionary theory predicts that preventing this "tragedy of the commons" requires a fixed spatial structure or other mechanisms that enable cells to interact preferentially with copies of themselves. Contrary to this expectation, we found that, in competition experiments, cells producing the diffusible growth factor interleukin-3 (IL3) resist invasion by non-producing mutant cells even in well-mixed populations, and that non-producers are driven to extinction instead. Using evolutionary game theory, we show that this outcome arises when the cost-to-benefit ratio of growth factor production falls below a critical threshold. We derive this tipping point analytically across the full parameter space of benefit function shape and group size and confirm that IL3 production in our experimental system satisfies this condition with a production cost less than 0.1% of the benefit conferred. These results demonstrate that efficient public good production alone can resolve the tragedy of the commons in populations of cells, and potentially in other biological systems.

papers.title: Macrophages use sub-micron actin ridges in phagocytosis of encapsulated fungal pathogens
papers.abstract: Ingestion and killing of pathogens by phagocytic cells is a key aspect of animal immunity. Cryptococcus neoformans is a major pathogen of AIDS patients that has a polysaccharide capsule that is critical for virulence. Phagocytic function is necessary for normal immunity to cryptococcal infection, and we sought to determine how Cryptococcus capsule prevents phagocytosis. In doing so, we discovered a new sub-micron actin structure, the ridge, that is present on macrophages, neutrophils and amoebae. Macrophages preferentially bind cryptococci via ridges and suppression of ridges is sufficient to prevent phagocytosis. Ridges are present on macrophages in vivo and are lost in interleukin 10 stimulated macrophages. The discovery and functional description of macrophage surface ridges fills a critical gap in our understanding of how phagocytes ingest encapsulated fungal pathogens, a crucial step in treating infection.

papers.title: Plasmodium rootlet SFA1 coordinates cell replication, apical polarity and cytoskeletal organisation during sexual development
papers.abstract: Rootlet fibres are evolutionarily conserved cytoskeletal structures involved in basal body positioning and cytoskeletal organisation in diverse eukaryotes. Plasmodium spps, undergo complex developmental transitions that require precise coordination of cell polarity, cytoskeletal remodelling and nuclear division. In Plasmodium striated fibre assemblin1 (SFA1) and SFA2 have been implicated in linking the centriolar plaque to nascent apical poles during schizogony and sporogony. However, their role in sexual development is unclear. Here we show SFA1 is absent from the male basal body but is present in female gametocytes, where it marks the polarity initiation site during zygote-to-ookinete differentiation. We also identify associations between SFA1, SFA2 and pellicle-associated proteins. Loss of sfa1 disrupts apical polarity, pellicle organisation and subpellicular microtubules, producing abnormal immotile ookinetes and affecting further sporozoite development, leading to complete loss of parasite transmission. Together, these findings support an important role for SFA1 in organising the cytoskeletal architecture required for malaria transmission.

papers.title: Substrate-induced asymmetry coordinates lipoprotein handover and abaucin trapping in Acinetobacter baumannii LolDF
papers.abstract: The homodimeric lipoprotein transporter LolDF supports outer-membrane biogenesis in Acinetobacter baumannii. How homodimeric LolDF generates directional lipoprotein transport, and how the reported two- and four-abaucin states are related, remain unclear. Using defined lipidated AbLolB and AbLolA, we show that substrate binding breaks LolF symmetry: LolFB primarily accommodates the lipid anchor, LolFA positions the adjacent polypeptide, and LolA docks asymmetrically through the LolF hook and an AbLolA-specific loop. C1 reconstruction of the wide abaucin state reveals non-equivalent central ligands, whereas C2 processing of the same particles averages this asymmetry; the two peripheral ligands form a stable inhibitory core, while the central sites are conditionally occupied in the expanded cavity. Abaucin inhibits ATPase activity and LolA-mediated transfer from substrate-associated LolDF, supporting a unified mechanism in which substrate-induced asymmetry organizes productive handover and its conformational plasticity is redirected during inhibition.

papers.title: A Unique Promoter Architecture Defines Menin-KMT2A Complex Selectivity
papers.abstract: Selective occupancy of chromatin-regulatory complexes is central to developmental gene regulation, yet the sequence determinants of this selectivity remain poorly understood. Using interpretable machine learning, we identify a composite promoter architecture comprising CpG islands flanked by several-kilobase A/T-rich domains (AT-flanks) that denotes high occupancy of the Menin-KMT2A histone-modifying complex at developmental and leukemia-associated genes. Genetic deletion and chromatin-contact analyses show that AT-flanks support KMT2A retention at linked CpG islands. We identify LEDGF as an A/T-rich DNA-associated protein required for Menin engagement at AT-flanks and sustained KMT2A promoter occupancy. AT-flank extent is associated with differential KMT2A loss following pharmacologic disruption of the Menin-KMT2A interaction, providing a genomic basis for heterogeneous target sensitivity to recently approved Menin inhibitors in acute leukemia. Beyond Menin-KMT2A, the same architecture distinguishes promoters with high canonical PRC1 occupancy across diverse cell types, revealing a shared sequence organization associated with distinct chromatin-regulatory states.

papers.title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding CagW, a conserved component of the Helicobacter pylori type IV secretion system, protects mice against H. pylori challenge
papers.abstract: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

papers.title: Experimental evolution reveals temporally opposing roles for Csu pili during Acinetobacter baumannii respiratory infection
papers.abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections observed in some patients. Recently, our laboratory developed a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection that enabled the identification of virulence factors specifically required for long-term lung persistence. To investigate how A. baumannii adapts during chronic pulmonary infection, we performed an experimental evolution study using this model. This approach revealed an unexpected role for the archaic chaperone-usher (Csu) pili in A. baumannii pathogenesis. At early time points, Csu expression reduced bacterial burdens in both acute and chronic pneumonia models, an effect associated with enhanced host inflammatory responses. In contrast, at later stages of chronic infection, Csu promoted bacterial persistence, potentially by facilitating adhesion to pulmonary epithelial cells. These opposing effects were conserved across two distinct A. baumannii clinical isolates. We also found that Csu contributes to bacterial colonization in a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) model in a strain-dependent manner. Together, these findings reveal an infection-stage-dependent role for Csu in A. baumannii pathogenesis, demonstrating that a bacterial surface structure can impair early colonization while promoting long-term persistence.

papers.title: A Vma13-targeted thiadiazole-succinimide disrupts V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis to block Candida albicans escape from macrophages
papers.abstract: Invasive candidiasis caused by Candida albicans is a life-threatening nosocomial infection with limited therapies and high morbidity and mortality among immunocompromised patients. Within host phagocytes, C. albicans catabolizes arginine to produce ammonia and fuels polyamine biosynthesis, which correlates with phagosomal alkalinization and yeast-to-hypha morphogenesis, facilitating macrophage escape and systemic dissemination. However, new antifungal strategies blocking this fungal escape remain scarce. Here, we characterize the thiadiazole-succinimide derivative ETSI, an arginine-dependent antifungal small molecule with minimal direct growth inhibition under arginine-free conditions yet robust anti-C. albicans activity in arginine-rich microenvironments mimicking the macrophage intracellular niche. Mechanistically, ETSI targets the vacuolar Vma13 to inhibit vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase), dissipating vacuolar proton (H+) gradients and leading to cytoplasmic H+ retention. The accumulated cytoplasmic H+ traps intracellular ammonia and blocks its external release, while impaired vacuolar metabolite sequestration further triggers cytotoxic accumulation of arginine and polyamine metabolites. This dual metabolic perturbation suppresses phagosomal alkalinization, retains C. albicans in yeast form and blocks macrophage escape. ETSI is the first small molecule blocking C. albicans escape via disrupted Vma13/V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis. This work identifies an intracellular metabolic vulnerability and establishes a niche-targeted antifungal strategy distinct from classic growth-suppressive drugs for treating invasive candidiasis.

papers.title: Megakaryocytic proteomic signatures define myeloproliferative neoplasms
papers.abstract: The classical Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are clonal stem cell disorders of the bone marrow with significant niche dysregulation driven in part by abnormal megakaryocytes. The three classical MPNs: polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET) and primary myelofibrosis (PMF), display established megakaryocytic morphological differences which aid in their diagnostic classification. The paucity of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow aspirate has previously limited a proteomic analysis of megakaryocytes in clinical samples. We aimed to undertake an unbiased proteomic analysis of in situ megakaryocytes from the bone marrow of patients with PV, ET, and PMF. Using a novel, deep visual proteomics strategy, we dissected and analyzed megakaryocytes from 60 MPN patients and 20 controls (patients with limited stage non-Hodgkin lymphoma who had uninvolved bone marrow). We reveal that megakaryocyte proteomics from MPN patients are distinct to those from control patients, and further, that the megakaryocytes from the three MPNs have unique, disease-specific signatures. The disease-specific megakaryocyte proteome highlights novel pathways of disease.

papers.title: Polygenic evolution towards a morning chronotype in modern humans
papers.abstract: Chronotype is a behavioural phenotype, and its phenotypic trend is considered to change at higher latitudes. In the current study, we performed a polygenic assessment of chronotype trend using associated single nucleotide polymorphisms identified by a genome wide-association study. We found that the phenotypic trend towards morningness increased drastically during the migration of anatomically modern humans above 20 degrees north. Furthermore, two types of latitudinal selection of morningness alleles contributed to establishing the trend towards the morning chronotype at higher latitudes. We propose that the trend towards morningness is stronger in present-day modern humans living above 20 degrees north than in Neanderthals.

papers.title: Estimating glioblastoma migration-to-proliferation ratio from single time-point MRI data via radial density distribution
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) tumors with a high migration-to-proliferation ratio (D/k) are associated with treatment resistance, motivating the estimation of D/k from routine pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data and the investigation of mechanisms underlying its heterogeneity across patients. Unlike previous approaches based on nested spherical approximations of enhancing and non-enhancing tumor volumes, we incorporate the spatial arrangement of the enhancing and non-enhancing tumor regions by deriving a 1D tumor density distribution from their segmentations and fitting a 1D reaction-diffusion model to estimate D/k. We achieved an error of under 5% when comparing our method to synthetic density distributions and found excellent correlation with synthetic tumor segmentations (Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.996). We then evaluated associations between patient-specific D/k values and their clinical, transcriptomic, and radiomic features. When applied to 102 pre-treatment MRI scans from the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2017 dataset, elevated D/k significantly correlated with reduced overall survival (log-rank p = 0.01), older age (p = 0.04), and a trend toward lower Karnofsky Performance Status (p = 0.059). In a subset of 91 patients with available microarray data, mesenchymal-like phenotypes consistently exhibited elevated D/k across three established molecular subtype classifications (p = 0.013, p = 0.055, and p = 0.127). Elastic Net regularization followed by overrepresentation analysis revealed an enrichment of glycosylation-related pathways among genes associated with D/k variability (p = 0.0123 and p = 0.0368). Furthermore, Multi-Omic Factor Analysis identified a radiomic factor correlated with D/k (r = 0.57, p = 4x10-9), with the highest-weighted features corresponding to smoothness of the non-enhancing tumor region on T2 and FLAIR.

papers.title: Distinct labeling of host and viral genomes highlights redistribution of nuclear proteins during HSV-1 infection
papers.abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) coordinates viral and cellular proteins during infection. While proteins associated with HSV-1 genomes have been identified, changes in proteins associated with the host genome during infection remain poorly understood. We adapted accelerated native isolation of proteins on nascent DNA (aniPOND) to label and purify cellular and viral DNA then identify associated proteins by mass spectrometry. Using this approach, we confirm observations that cellular transcription, DNA replication, and repair proteins are enriched on viral genomes after the onset of viral DNA replication. We assessed how protein interactions with cellular DNA change during infection relative to protein abundance. Targets of the viral E3 ubiquitin ligase, ICP0, are depleted from the nucleus and cellular genome during infection. Transcription regulatory factors, Pol II, and the proteasome are depleted from the host genome, while association with DNA damage response and nuclear pore proteins increases. We also provide evidence for HSV-1 disruption of ribosome biogenesis. Results demonstrate reorganization of the nucleus during infection and validate this technique to identify changes to host genome-associated factors during infection.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics re-analysis of public sequencing and metabolomics repositories defines the mucosal immune and metabolic landscape of Helicobacter pylori infection and supports CagW as a rational mRNA-LNP vaccine antigen
papers.abstract: Background. Helicobacter pylori colonises 40-45% of the global population, is a WHO Group I carcinogen, and is increasingly hard to eradicate amid rising resistance; no vaccine is licensed. CagW, a VirB6-family cagPAI component, has been advanced as a DNA-vaccine antigen that protects mice; a codon-optimised CagW-Fc mRNA in lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNP) is a candidate antigen design intended to engage humoral and cellular immunity. To define the infected gastric mucosal niche in which such a vaccine must operate, we mined public sequencing, single-cell and metabolomics repositories. Methods. NCBI GEO, MetaboLights and NCBI Protein were interrogated. Bulk transcriptomes of H. pylori-infected vs uninfected gastric epithelial cells (GSE295523; 24 libraries: HGC27, AGS, MKN45, GES-1) were re-analysed with a cell-line-blocked design; DEGs (BH-adjusted) were annotated via g:Profiler (GO, KEGG, Reactome) and 13 functional signatures scored. Single-cell composition was quantified from a mouse gastric scRNA-seq atlas (GSE224840; 16,434 cells) and sorted gastric CD8+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) vs splenic memory T cells (GSE216894). Targeted gastric metabolomics was re-analysed for epithelial ornithine decarboxylase (Odc) deletion (MTBLS3235) and cystathionine-gamma-lyase (Cth) deletion (MTBLS2851). CagW conservation was computed across 400 NCBI records (286 variants) with Kyte-Doolittle topology and four B cell epitope scales. Results. Infection induced 326 up- and 115 down-regulated genes (FDR 1), dominated by TNF/NF-kappaB (KEGG hsa04668, P=5.5x10-11), integrated stress response (ATF4-CHAC1-DDIT3-TRIB3-ASNS) and Th17 chemokines (CXCL8 +3.43, CCL20 +1.32, CXCL1 +1.30, IL23A +1.02). MHC-I presentation rose (Delta-z +0.76; MHC-II unchanged); the arginine/polyamine module (SLC7A1 +1.19, ARG2 +1.33, SAT1 +1.50, ODC1 +0.58) was co-induced. scRNA-seq showed immune expansion in infected mucosa (39.8% vs 21.2% cells; OR 2.46; cell-level frequencies reported descriptively because cells are not independent; direction confirmed at sample level, n=4 vs 4), driven by plasmacytoid DCs (OR 8.9), neutrophils (OR 3.0), macrophages (OR 2.7) and cDCs (OR 2.1), with epithelial de-differentiation. Gastric CD8+ TRM cells showed a residency-effector program (Itgae +6.2, Cd69 +2.3, Gzmb +4.8, Ifng +5.3) with egress-gene loss (Sell -11.4, S1pr1 -9.7, Klf2 -5.2). Metabolomics confirmed both nodes: Odc deletion raised arginine (+3.08) and Cth deletion raised spermidine (+0.40) while lowering leukotriene B4 (-0.33). CagW was conserved across 286 variants (median 98.3% identity; 96.4% residues >=95% conserved), carried four transmembrane helices, and showed a surface-biased conserved epitope envelope at residues 505-530 and 63-79. Conclusions. Public multi-omics define an NF-kappaB/ATF4-driven, Th17-polarised, metabolically stressed niche where antigen-presenting cells expand, epithelium de-differentiates, and CD8+ TRM cells act locally. Here CagW is exceptional among cagPAI antigens: near-universal conservation plus an accessible, conserved surface. These findings provide a systems-level rationale for prioritising CagW as a conserved, epitope-accessible vaccine antigen and inform next-generation multi-antigen designs.

papers.title: Systematic analysis reveals an Mln1-dependent trade-off between metabolic flexibility and thermotolerance in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: During infection, fungal pathogens must adapt to multiple environmental challenges, including changes in temperature, nutrient availability, and immune stress. Although transcriptional regulators are central to these adaptations, how individual regulators contribute to distinct environmental responses and how these responses are functionally interconnected remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functions of infection-associated transcription factors under distinct host-relevant conditions in Cryptococcus neoformans. Integrating in vivo expression profiling with infectivity data from signature-tagged mutagenesis, we prioritized 24 transcription factors, 12 of which were induced under host-mimicking conditions. Initial functional analyses revealed distinct roles for these transcription factors in adaptation to temperature, carbon, and nitrogen availability. Further characterization of Mln1, a fungal basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, uncovered an unexpected connection between carbon source adaptation and thermotolerance. Mig1-dependent repression limited MLN1 expression in the presence of glucose, whereas Mln1 accumulated in the nucleus in the presence of trehalose or ethanol, but not glucose. Loss of MLN1 impaired carbon-starvation gene expression and growth on non-preferred carbon sources, particularly trehalose. Conversely, mln1{Delta} cells accumulated more intracellular trehalose and exhibited enhanced thermotolerance, yet showed reduced melanization, titan cell formation, virulence in Drosophila, and brain fungal burden in mice. Together, these results suggest that Mln1 contributes to metabolic flexibility and fungal virulence while differentially influencing thermotolerance. More broadly, these findings highlight a potential physiological trade-off between nutrient utilization and stress resistance, suggesting that these adaptive processes may be interconnected in fungal pathogens.

papers.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress
papers.abstract: Host-parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host-pathogen coevolutionary trajectories.

papers.title: DGM Is Dead; Long Live DGM-Star! A Quantization-Theoretic Approach to Gamma Rate Discretization
papers.abstract: Modeling substitution rate heterogeneity as a discretized Gamma distribution is standard in phylogenetic inference. Ferretti et al. (2026) have recently demonstrated that the most commonly used equiprobable Gamma rate discretization, known simply as the discrete Gamma model (DGM), substantially overestimates average branch lengths in reconstructed phylogenies when the true rates are drawn from a continuous Gamma distribution. We propose an alternative method to discretize the Gamma rate distribution that considerably reduces the bias in estimated branch lengths and can be used as a drop-in replacement for the standard DGM. The method works especially well on large trees with short branches, yielding up to a 20-fold reduction in bias on simulated phylogenies. It is developed by applying quantization-theoretic tools to the analysis of a simplified star-phylogeny abstraction introduced by Ferretti et al. (2026), where the new method is unbiased by construction. We explain Ferretti et al.'s counterintuitive observation that increasing the number of rate categories can exacerbate the bias of the standard DGM, even though this should in principle make DGM a better approximation to the continuous case, and offer our method as an immediately available alternative.

papers.title: Joint QTL mapping reveals patterns of pleiotropy across structured environments in budding yeast
papers.abstract: Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping studies in model organisms have long been used to infer the structure of genotype-phenotype maps. However, prior work has largely focused on analyzing the genetic architecture of complex traits individually. Here, we sought to instead infer genotype-phenotype maps for a large set of related phenotypes simultaneously. To do so, we used bulk assays to measure the competitive fitness of each of 100,000 individuals from a large budding yeast QTL mapping panel across a set of 101 phenotypes related by a ``hub-and-perturbation'' pattern, and then used a forward search approach to jointly infer the genetic basis of all phenotypes together. Our results reveal complex patterns of pleiotropy in the genetic architecture of these traits. We find that these patterns of pleiotropy reflect the structure of the environmental relationships as well as functional information about individual variants and the interactions between them. This suggests that high-throughput QTL mapping across structured environments can help uncover biologically meaningful genetic interactions, along with their variation across related environmental contexts.
